chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
title: Levee camps and the blues singers; a medicine show with Jim Jackson
summary: He explains levee-camp entertainment for Tampa Red and others, and recalls taking over for Stepin Fetchit on a medicine show.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: All I know of Lonny Johnson/was with Victoria Spivey, yes. The first time was to know that he made the records of "Furniture Man Blues". All I know of Helen Humes when the mother brought her from Louisville, Kentucky, to come in to the thing and Lonny Johnson came in there. But you must remember that Lonny Johnson was a big star then, along with Leroy Carr, ScrappER Blackwell, and those peoples, and Tampa Reds. You must remember those peoples come up through the levee camps. Peoples have never told you what a levee camp was because during the time when the Mississippi River was going through the floods and what have you, the people would go along to try to fix up so that the floods wouldn't go into the areas that would mess up the farmlands and what have you, all the way down. The Mississippi started in Minnesota and come on down all through St. Paul and come on down and come on down through these areas. But then people were what you call camp followers so when people were working they had to have some sort of entertainment, so you got the Tampa Reds, you got the Scrap' Wells,* you got these peoples that come around to entertain these people. After these people had gotten through doing their chores on a Friday or Saturday, then they had their fish fries. Then they'd have the other things and I do remember that I, in my life,

I took over for Step'n Fetchit. I took over for him on a medicine show. I worked with a guitar player, you see, Jiving Jim Jackson. He wrote a tune, "I'm Going to Move to Kansas City" and the other guitarist played a double guitar. I remember that, and we were out on a medicine show and we sold medicine, 50¢, a cure-all. I do remember this.
